title: Woman credits cops with saving her life
article: A Whitby woman is crediting Durham police with saving her life after a stand-off in which a knife-wielding man was shot dead.
"If they hadn't been there, I'd be dead," Susan Wilson said in the aftermath of a drama that left 42-year-old Dave Noble dead.

Police went to a home on Bluebell Crescent just after 1 a.m. Saturday in response to a 911 call made by Ms. Wilson, 41. She said she and a friend had been accosted by an enraged Mr. Noble, who beat her male friend and then dragged her into her house.

Ms. Wilson said she was chased around her house by the knife- carrying Mr. Noble, who was confronted by responding police officers as he tried to drag her back inside after she'd exited through the front door.
Neighbours described efforts by cops to calm Mr. Noble and get him to release the woman before the fatal shot was fired.

The province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) is currently looking into the shooting. It's the second fatal shooting of a civilian by Durham cops in a month. On March 6, Elyas Bariali, 29, was shot during a confrontation with officers in Oshawa.
The SIU, which investigates police actions that result in death or injury to civilians, ruled the officer who shot Mr. Bariali acted appropriately.
Both incidents highlight the quickness with which situations can become life-and-death decisions for cops, said Durham Regional Police Association president Doug Cavanaugh.
"There are snap decisions you have to make out there," he said.
Mr. Cavanaugh acknowledged it's inevitable that questions about use of force will be raised when deadly force is employed by cops.

Such was the case in Mr. Bariali's death. His family contends other methods should have been employed to help subdue Mr. Bariali, a schizophrenic who advanced toward cops clutching a screwdriver after a man was stabbed in a fight at a Drew Street rooming house.
"What happened there was not justified," said Emal Bariali, the dead man's brother, shortly after the release of the SIU finding.

Police Services Board Chair Doug Moffatt said use of force tactics and technology - such as much-touted Tasers, which deliver a strong electrical shock that incapacitates targets - have been the focus of board discussions. Expanding Durham's limited use of Tasers has been considered, he said.
Deputy-chief Chuck Mercier said, for the most part, the jury remains out on Taser use in Ontario. Members of the tactical unit and some other Durham cops now carry the devices, he said.
"There's all kinds of technology out there, but you have to evaluate the practicality of it," Deputy-Chief Mercier said.
Mr. Cavanaugh cautioned that devices like Tasers may not be an all-encompassing, non-lethal option for cops facing life-or-death situations.
"I would like to look at it more, but I don't think it's the be all and end all," he said.
